summary: Defines the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP), by which MPLS routers tell each other what labels they use so traffic can be forwarded along normally routed paths. It is a Draft Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5036 defines the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP), which lets MPLS routers agree on the labels they use to forward packets. Routers discover neighbors, establish a session, and exchange label mappings so that labeled traffic can follow the same paths as IP routing.

questions: how do mpls routers exchange labels
how do ldp peers establish a session
subtitle: How MPLS routers agree on the labels they stick on packets, so traffic can follow normally routed paths.

tldr.problem: In MPLS, two neighboring Label Switching Routers (LSRs) must agree on what each label means before they can forward traffic by label. They need a standard way to tell each other.
tldr.mechanism: LDP has routers find each other with UDP Hello messages, open a TCP session, negotiate parameters, and then exchange label mappings that tie a Forwarding Equivalence Class to a label.
tldr.outcome: This document is a Draft Standard that replaces RFC 3036 and has since been updated by RFC 6720, RFC 6790, RFC 7358 and RFC 7552. It is the base specification of LDP.

today: RFC 5036 is a Draft Standard that replaces RFC 3036 and is updated by RFC 6720, RFC 6790, RFC 7358 and RFC 7552. It remains the base specification of LDP.

sections.title: What LDP Is For
sections.content:
The MPLS architecture (RFC 3031) says that two Label Switching Routers must agree on the meaning of the labels used to forward traffic between and through them. A label distribution protocol is the set of procedures by which one LSR tells another about the label bindings it has made. The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) is one such protocol, defined to support MPLS forwarding along normally routed paths.

LDP is the set of procedures and messages by which LSRs establish Label Switched Paths (LSPs) through a network, mapping network-layer routing information directly to data-link layer switched paths. An LSP may end at a directly attached neighbor, which is comparable to IP hop-by-hop forwarding, or at a network egress node. The protocol was first published as RFC 3036 in January 2001, and this document replaces it.

Two LSRs that exchange label and FEC mapping information are LDP peers, and there is an LDP session between them. LDP messages fall into four categories: discovery messages, session messages, advertisement messages, and notification messages.
sections.plainLanguage:
LDP allows neighboring routers to agree on what each label means so they can forward packets using labels instead of looking up full addresses at every hop. This establishes label-switched paths that follow the same routes chosen by IP routing.

Neighbors discover each other, set up a session, exchange label mappings, and notify each other of errors or changes.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
LDP associates a Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) with each LSP. The FEC says which packets are mapped to that LSP. This specification defines the Address Prefix FEC element, a prefix of any length. A packet matches an LSP when its destination address begins with the LSP's prefix. If multiple LSPs match, the one with the longest matching prefix is used.

A label space is either per interface or per platform. An LDP Identifier names one label space of an LSR and consists of a globally unique 4-octet LSR identifier and a 2-octet label space identifier (both zero for the platform-wide label space), written as <LSR Id>:<label space id>.

An LSR that advertises more than one label space uses a separate LDP session and TCP connection for each.
sections.plainLanguage:
A Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) groups packets that should be treated the same way, such as all packets going to a particular address prefix. LDP binds each such group to a label.

Each label space on a router has a unique identifier, and sessions are established per label space between peers.

sections.title: Discovery, Sessions, and Operations
sections.content:
Routers find peers by discovery. In Basic Discovery, an LSR periodically sends LDP Link Hellos as UDP packets to the well-known LDP multicast group on an interface. In Extended Discovery, an LSR sends Targeted Hellos to a specific address to establish sessions with non-directly connected LSRs. Receiving a Hello creates a Hello adjacency with a negotiated hold timer.

Hellos trigger session establishment. The LSRs determine transport addresses and the one with the higher transport address plays the active role, connecting to TCP port 646; the other is passive. They exchange Initialization messages to negotiate parameters such as protocol version, label distribution method, and timer values. If parameters are acceptable, they exchange KeepAlive messages and the session becomes OPERATIONAL.

LDP supports two label advertisement modes: Downstream Unsolicited and Downstream on Demand. Label distribution control is either Independent or Ordered. Label retention is either Liberal or Conservative. Appendix A of the RFC is the authoritative description of these procedures.
sections.plainLanguage:
Routers announce their presence with hello messages sent either to neighbors on a link or to specific addresses. When two routers learn of each other, they open a TCP connection, agree on session parameters, and confirm with keepalives to keep the session active.

They then exchange label bindings according to negotiated rules for when and how labels are advertised and retained.

sections.title: Message and TLV Format
sections.content:
Every LDP PDU starts with a 10-octet header containing Version (version 1), PDU Length, and the sender's LDP Identifier. It is followed by one or more messages. Most information is carried in TLVs (Type-Length-Value) with a 2-octet type (including U and F behavior bits) and a 2-octet length.

Each message has a common header with a Message Type, Message Length, and Message ID. A Label Mapping message carries a FEC TLV and a Label TLV, and when responding to a Label Request it includes the original Message ID. Hello messages include Common Hello Parameters indicating hold time and whether the hello is targeted.

Key message types include Hello, Initialization, KeepAlive, Address, Address Withdraw, Label Mapping, Label Request, Label Withdraw, Label Release, Label Abort Request, and Notification.
sections.plainLanguage: All LDP messages follow a structured binary format with a header identifying the sender, followed by messages that each contain their type, length, and identifier. Most fields are encoded as TLVs, making the protocol extensible while still allowing unrecognized TLVs to be handled safely.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
LDP's UDP-based discovery is vulnerable to spoofed Hellos, which can cause sessions to time out. Defenses include accepting Basic Hellos only on interfaces to trusted directly connected LSRs, ignoring Basic Hellos not sent to the multicast group, and filtering Extended Hellos with access lists.

TCP session traffic is protected by the TCP MD5 Signature Option for authenticity and integrity. LDP provides no privacy for label distribution; its authenticity and integrity protection is intended to be at least as good as that of the routing protocols themselves.

For denial-of-service protection, implementations should be careful with promiscuous TCP listens and use access lists at network edges to protect interior LSRs.
sections.plainLanguage:
To protect LDP, routers should only accept discovery messages from trusted neighbors and use message authentication on TCP sessions. Access controls can help prevent denial-of-service attacks.

The protocol does not encrypt label distribution messages, so it assumes the control network is trusted or protected by other means.
